name: Tomas Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. To begin, could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the die-cutting line at Eastfield Packaging, which turns big sheets of corrugated board into shipping boxes for online shops. I start at 6, swap the cutting dies, set the feed and the stacker, and watch the quality of the cuts. Some days it's the same box for eight hours, and other days it's six short runs and my hands never stop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy getting the changeover down to under twenty minutes, it's a bit of a sport with my crew. What wears me out is the dust and the noise, and the bad days when a stack topples and we spend an hour picking board off the floor. Also the rush before Christmas, which is brutal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right, honestly. My daughter has shown me a few things on her phone and they save some time, but nobody's life changes. I'd tell the guys at the plant not to lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fairly relaxed. A die-cutter still needs a person to set it up and spot a bad cut, and nobody has solved that. If anything, the extra online orders keep us busy, and I'm four years from retiring, so I'd glide in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and take the normal overtime before Christmas. I'd keep the monthly savings at 150 and let the mortgage finish in two years. I'd also let my daughter Niamh teach me a few more tricks for the spreadsheet we use for the shift schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It's what I'd choose if I could choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your plant is tied to online shopping. How secure does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fairly secure, because every shop sends boxes. But if the big online retailers start making their own boxes, or ship in bags, we'd have trouble. I watch the order board on the wall like some people watch the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Niamh set me up with one, and I use it to write polite emails to customers who send me bad drawings, and to fix spreadsheet formulas. I check everything it says, because the first time it told me a die was the wrong size and I nearly believed it.

say: I'd say it sounds about right, and I'd tell the guys not to **lose sleep** over it.
Some tools save time, but nobody's **life** changes.
think: I'd be fairly **relaxed**, because a die-cutter still needs a person to set it up.
Online orders keep us busy, so I could **glide** into retirement in four years.
do: Carry on as normal and take the **pre-Christmas overtime**.
Keep saving **150 a month** while the mortgage finishes in two years.
Let my daughter Niamh show me more **spreadsheet tricks**.
feel: **Settled**, the future I'd choose if I could choose.
S0.quote: A die-cutter still needs a person
fieldNote: **Calm for real reasons**: his skill is still needed, orders are steady and the mortgage ends soon.
**Watches the order board** like a weather forecast, which shows a pressure he doesn't hide.
**Uses AI carefully**: he checks everything after it once gave a wrong die size.

steps.text: Take the usual overtime before Christmas
Save 150 a month while the mortgage runs out
Ask Niamh to teach me more spreadsheet and email tricks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be smart. The office goes first. Quoting, ordering board and scheduling all go to software. On the floor I'd say we'll get more cameras and sensors, and the rest comes slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the line stays mine for a while, but my day gets different. If software does the scheduling and checks the quality, a team lead's job gets thinner, and the plant might want fewer leads. I'd say I have a decent chance of being fine, but it's not a sure thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the plant's training on the new scheduling system, since it'll be on my screen sooner or later. I'd pay down the mortgage faster, aiming for 12 months to clear it. And I'd spend a bit of time learning the quality camera system, so I'm the one the crew asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not scared. A bit like when we moved from the old manual feed to the automatic one, and everybody thought half of us would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your plant would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quoting and the scheduling, for sure, and the stock ordering. Probably the quality checks too, because a camera sees a cracked edge faster than I do. The die swaps and the jams stay with people longer, as far as I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your wife Helen say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says I worry too much. She runs her own chair at a salon, so her income moves around a bit, and she'd say let's keep our spending steady and see. She's probably right, but one of us has to have the lists.

The office goes first, while the floor gets **cameras and sensors** slowly.
think: The line stays mine for a while, but a **team lead** job gets thinner.
I'd say I have a decent chance of being fine, but it's **not a sure thing**.
do: Take the plant's training on the new **scheduling system**.
Pay down the mortgage faster and clear it in **12 months**.
Learn the quality **camera system** so the crew asks me.
feel: **Uneasy but not scared**, like when the plant switched to automatic feed and everyone feared for jobs.
S1.quote: The die swaps and the jams
fieldNote: **Measured**: he accepts change, sorts which tasks go first and picks a spot to be useful.
**Home income** moves a bit because his wife runs her own chair at a salon.
**Mortgage first** is his way to gain security.

steps.text: Take the plant's training on the new scheduling system
Pay down the mortgage in the next 12 months
Learn the quality camera system so the crew asks me first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need adults in the room, now. Two years is not enough for the plant, the town or the government. I'd ask the manager for a meeting with the crew, and I'd tell him I'd rather hear bad news early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious, to be honest. The planning and quoting would go in 2028, the plant would need fewer people overall, and the robots would come for the line in 2031. I'd be 60 then, with maybe three years to go before I could draw a pension, and that's a nasty gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending and put every spare euro into savings, aiming for eight months. I'd ask the plant to put me on the first robot-feeder project, because somebody has to set up the line for the robots. I'd also ask the pension office exactly what retiring at 61 would cost me, in actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Not panicking, but the sort of feeling you get when the order board goes quiet in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots around 2031. What does that mean for a die-cutter operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my hands-on work is safe a little longer. The robots come three years after the thinking AI, and a die swap is awkward even for a clever robot. But three years goes quickly, and the plant could automate a simple line sooner than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think has to do something about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All of us. The government first, to prepare people. The plant second, to tell the truth. And us third, to ask and not stay quiet. If any one of those fails, we all pay.

say: I'd say we need **adults in the room** now, because two years is too short for the plant.
I'd ask the manager for a **crew meeting** and tell him I'd rather hear bad news early.
think: Planning and quoting go in 2028 and the line follows in **2031**, leaving a nasty gap before my pension.
The plant could automate a simple line **sooner** than I'd like.
do: Cut spending and aim for **eight months** of savings.
Ask to join the first **robot-feeder project**, because somebody must set up the line.
Get exact numbers on **retiring at 61** from the pension office.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, like when the order board goes quiet in January.
fieldNote: **Anxious but organised**: he turns worry into a list and a plan.
**Gap before pension** is the sharpest issue, not the technology alone.
**Shared responsibility**: he names government, plant and workers all together.

steps.text: Cut spending and aim for eight months of savings
Cancel the holiday and the gym membership this year
Ask to be on the first robot-feeder project
Ask the pension office what retiring at 61 would cost

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is breathing room, and we should use it well. I'd talk to the manager about training, and I'd tell the crew to learn something that has hands and a screen together. Don't wait for a flyer from the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I think is that it's manageable for me. AI hits the office when I'm 63 and the line when I'm 66, and by then I'd be in retirement or only part-time. The younger people on my crew are the ones with the real problem, since they have decades left and a mortgage like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the mortgage in two years, build up six months of savings and keep working to 62. I'd do the plant's training on any automation, because it can't hurt. If I get offered a part-time role as a trainer when I retire, I'd probably take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better, honestly. Like finding out the storm will arrive in a few days instead of a few hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you change from the two-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd have been in survival mode. With five, I can pay the house off, learn the new system and still have a spare month or two in the bank. A five-year warning is the difference between being pushed and walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to younger people on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the quality camera system, the scheduling software and the basics of the robot feeder. Don't pick hands or screens, learn both. And save something every month, even a small amount, because it adds up faster than you think.

say: I'd say five years is **breathing room**, and we should use it well.
I'd tell the crew to learn something with **hands and a screen** together.
think: It's **manageable for me**, because AI reaches the line when I'm 66 and I'd be retired by then.
The **younger people** on my crew have decades left and mortgages like mine.
do: Finish the **mortgage** in two years and build six months of savings.
Do the plant's **automation training** because it can't hurt.
Take a part-time **trainer role** after retirement if offered.
feel: **A bit better**, like learning a storm arrives in a few days rather than hours.
fieldNote: **Time makes him calmer** but he keeps worrying about younger colleagues with mortgages.
**Concrete**: pay off the house first, then learn the new systems.
**Mentor streak**: advice to learn both hands and screens.

steps.text: Finish the mortgage within two years
Do the plant's training on any new automation
Work until 62 and build six months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the kind of warning you wish every big change came with. Ten years gives everybody time. I'd say it to my crew, and I'd say it to the council as well, since towns like ours need to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's more or less fine. I'd be retired and pottering about. The worry is the young ones and the town, because an automated packaging plant employs far fewer people, and our high street depends on those pay packets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned, retire at 62, and keep the mortgage-free house and a bit of savings. I'd probably volunteer as a mentor for the apprentices at the technical school. And I'd vote for the local candidate who has a real plan for jobs in the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, pretty calm. It's the world my grandkids will live in more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you well past retirement. What is the worry then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension and the town. If the plant gets smaller and the town loses its pay packets, the shops close and my pension buys less. I'd keep an eye on how the council handles it, and I'd want some say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently now, knowing you have so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd keep my eyes open, and I'd keep my daughter Niamh nearby, because she knows what's coming with the tech. Ten years is long enough that I don't need to run, only to be ready.

say: I'd say it's the kind of warning every big change should come with, since ten years gives **everybody time**.
Towns like ours need to **plan**, and I'd tell the council.
think: For me it's **fine**: I'd be retired and pottering about.
My worry is the **town**, because an automated plant means fewer pay packets for the high street.
do: Retire at **62** as planned and keep the paid-off house.
Volunteer as a **mentor** for apprentices at the technical school.
Vote for a local candidate with a real **jobs plan** for the town.
feel: **Calm**, since it's more my grandchildren's world than mine.
S4.quote: The worry is the young ones
fieldNote: **Calm by timing**: his job and pension are safe, so the concern moves to the high street.
**Civic minded**: mentoring and voting for a local jobs plan.
**Pension value** depends on the town's health, which he keeps in view.

steps.text: Retire at 62 and keep the house and savings
Mentor apprentices at the technical school

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the gap before my pension. What would help is clear information early, a retraining scheme that pays while you learn, and a pension that lets me go at 61 without a huge penalty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a die-cutter has to do with the world. Every parcel that arrives at somebody's door comes in a box that a person like me set up. I'm proud of that, and I'd like us not to be forgotten.

portrait: **Tomas** is a 58-year-old die-cutting line lead at a corrugated packaging plant, about four years from retirement.
He is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, **open to change**, and uses AI now and then with careful checking.
His mortgage ends in two years, he has about **three months** of savings, and his wife's salon income moves around.
He stays calm in the slow pictures and turns **anxious** in the two-year picture, where a gap opens before his pension.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because of the gap before his pension.
whatWouldHelp: **Early, clear information**, paid retraining, and a pension that lets him leave at 61 without a big penalty.
